en: One should meditate upon this syllable "Om" as the Udgītha;
for one begins the chant with "Om.
Here follows its further explanation. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1)
Of these beings, the earth is the essence;
of the earth, water is the essence;
of water, plants are the essence.
Of herbs, man is the essence;
of man, speech is the essence;
of speech, the Ṛgveda is the essence.
The Ṛg-veda has the Sāman as its essence;
the Sāman has the Udgītha as its essence.
This very Udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth.
"What is the Ṛk? What is the Sāman? What is the Udgītha?"—thus it was deliberated. ChU 1.1.4.
Speech indeed is the Ṛc;
breath is the Sāman;
the syllable "Om" is the Udgītha.
Now, this is indeed a union: speech and breath, and the Ṛg-verse and the Sāman-chant.
This couple is united in this syllable "Om.
Indeed, when a couple comes together, they fulfill each other's desire.
He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7)
This, indeed, is the syllable of assent; for whatever one assents to, one says "Om.
This very thing, namely assent, is prosperity.
Verily, he becomes a fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.8)
Therefore, this triple knowledge proceeds thus:
one causes the announcement with "Oṃ," and one recites the praise with "Oṃ."
He sings the Udgītha with "Om," for the sake of honoring this very syllable, by means of its greatness and its essence.
Therefore, both perform it:
he who knows this thus, and he who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are indeed distinct.
"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful. This, indeed, is the further explanation of this very syllable.

Once, when the gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, were contending with one another, the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, "By this we shall overcome them. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.1)
They meditated upon the breath of the nose as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, one smells both the fragrant and the foul with it.
For he is pierced by evil.
Then they indeed worshipped speech as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one speaks both the true and the false.
For she has been pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the eye as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly.
For this is pierced by evil. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.4)
Then they venerated the ear as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one hears both that which is worth hearing and that which is not worth hearing.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the mind as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one conceives both that which is to be conceived and that which is not to be conceived.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then, they meditated upon that very breath which is the principal one as the Udgītha.
When the Asuras struck it, they were shattered, just as a clod of earth would shatter upon striking a solid stone. 1.2.7.

Just as a clod of earth striking a solid stone is shattered, even so is he shattered who desires evil against one who knows this, and he who seeks to harm him; for such a person is like that clod of earth against the stone. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.8)
By this [breath], one perceives neither fragrance nor foul odor,
for it is free from evil.
Whatever it eats and whatever it drinks, by that it sustains the other vital breaths.
Indeed, it is only after not finding this [Self] at the end that one departs;
for at the end, one simply opens [the mouth]. Thus ends the first chapter, second section.
Aṅgiras meditated upon that as the Udgītha;
it is he indeed whom they consider to be Aṅgirasa, because he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga).
Therefore, Bṛhaspati meditated upon that Udgītha.
Indeed, they consider him to be Bṛhaspati;
for speech is the Great (Bṛhatī), and he is its lord (pati).
Therefore, he meditated upon that Udgītha as Āyāsya;
for they consider him indeed to be Āyāsya,
because he moves from the mouth (āsya).
By this means, Baka Dālbhya came to know it;
he became the Udgātṛ priest for the people of Naimiṣa,
and he used to obtain all desires for them by singing.
"Verily, one who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha, becomes the attainer of all desires.
This is with reference to the self. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.14)
Now, with reference to the deities:
one should meditate upon that very sun which shines as the Udgītha.
Indeed, rising, it sings the Udgītha for the sake of all creatures.
Rising, it dispels the fear of darkness.
He who knows this indeed becomes a dispeller of the fear of darkness. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.1)
This one here and that one yonder are indeed the same:
this is warm, and that is warm.
They call this one "sound" (svara), and they call that one "echo" (pratyāsvara).
Therefore, one should indeed meditate upon this Udgītha and that [Udgītha].
Now, one should indeed meditate upon the vyāna breath as the udgītha. That which one breathes out is the prāṇa; that which one breathes in is the apāna.
Now, that which is the junction of the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (apāna) is the diffused breath (vyāna). That which is the diffused breath is speech.
Therefore, one utters speech without breathing out or breathing in.
That speech which is Ṛk, therefore one utters the Ṛk without breathing out or breathing in;
that which is Ṛk is Sāman.
Therefore, one sings the Sāman without breathing out or breathing in.
That which is the Sāman is the Udgītha;
therefore, one sings the Udgītha without breathing out or breathing in.

Therefore, whatever other vigorous actions there are—such as the churning of fire, the running in a race, or the drawing of a stiff bow—he performs them without breathing in or breathing out. For this reason, one should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the *vyāna* breath itself. (ChU 1.3.5)
Now, one should indeed meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*, namely: *ut*, *gī*, and *tha*. The syllable *ut* is breath (*prāṇa*), for by means of breath one rises up.
Speech is *gīḥ*; for they call speech *giraḥ*. Food is *tham*.
For on food indeed all this is supported. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.6)
Heaven is indeed the *ut*,
the intermediate space is the *gīr*,
and the earth is the *tham*.
Āditya is the *ut*;
Vāyu is the *gīḥ*;
Agni is the *tham*.
The Sāmaveda is indeed *ut*;
the Yajurveda is *gīḥ*;
the Ṛgveda is *tham*.
Speech milks for him that milk which is the milk of speech;
he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon these syllables of the Udgītha as "ut," "gī," and "tha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.7)
Now, indeed, it is the fulfillment of one's blessing.
One should worship [the deities] as "approaches. With whatever Sāman one intends to chant, one should meditate upon that Sāman.
One should meditate upon that Ṛṣi who is the seer of the Ṛc in which one is to recite it; and one should approach that deity whom one is about to praise. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.9)
One should meditate upon that metre with which one intends to praise;
one should meditate upon that Stoma with which one is about to praise. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.10)
In whichever direction one intends to praise, toward that direction one should run.

Having approached the Self at the very end, let him praise while meditating on his desire and remaining vigilant; for that desire for which he praises will surely be fulfilled for him—whatever desire he may have when he praises, whatever desire he may have when he praises. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.12)
One should meditate upon this syllable "Om" as the Udgītha; for one begins the chanting with "Om. This is its further explanation. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.4.1)

The gods, fearing death, entered the threefold knowledge. They covered themselves with the meters; because they covered themselves with them, that is the reason for the "metrical" nature (*chandastva*) of the meters. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.4.2)
Thereupon, as one might look for a fish in water, Death looked for them in the Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Yajurveda.
But having found them, they rose above the Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Yajurveda, and entered into the very tone itself.
When one encounters a Ṛg verse, one utters "Om" as a high-pitched sound; likewise for a Sāman chant and likewise for a Yajus formula.
This syllable is indeed the very tone, this is the immortal, the fearless.
Having entered that, the gods became immortal.
He who, knowing this thus, utters the syllable Om, enters that very syllable—the sound, the immortal, the fearless.
Having entered it, he becomes immortal like the immortal gods. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.4.5)
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
Yonder sun, verily, is the Udgītha;
it is this Praṇava, for it moves along sounding "Om."
"It was precisely this that I meditated upon; therefore, you are my only son," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"You must turn back the rays;
then indeed many sons shall be yours."
Thus with reference to the deities. ChUp 1.5.2.
Now, with reference to the self: one should meditate upon that which is this chief vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*.
For it goes forth sounding "Om."
"It was precisely this that I sang to; therefore, you are my only one," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"Sing to the breaths as the Plurality, for then many indeed shall be mine. ChUp 1.5.4.
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
For even from the Hotṛ’s seat, he can rectify a poorly performed Udgītha—yes, he can rectify it. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.5)
This very thing is the *ṛc*; Agni is the *sāman*.
Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. This [earth] is the Sāman;
Agni is the Ama.
That is Sāman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1)
The intermediate space is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the wind is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being superimposed upon the *ṛc*.
The intermediate space itself is the *sā*,
and the wind is the *ama*.
That is the Sāman. ChU 1.6.2.
The sky is indeed the Ṛg;
the sun is the Sāman.
Thus, this Sāman is supported upon that Ṛg.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superimposed upon the Ṛc.
The sky is indeed that (Sāman), and the sun is the *ama*.
That is the Sāman. ChU 1.6.3.
The stars are the *ṛc*,
the moon is the *sāman*;
thus this *sāman* is superposed upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superposed upon the Ṛc; the stars are the Sāman,
and the moon is the Āma.
That is the Sāman. ChU 1.6.4.
Now, that which is the white light of the sun is the *ṛc*;
and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superimposed upon the Ṛc.
Now, that which is the white light of this sun is indeed *sā*;
and that which is blue, exceedingly black, is *ama*.
That is *sāman*.
Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, down even to the tips of his nails, is entirely composed of gold.
His eyes are like a lotus flower that is as yellow as the buttocks of a monkey;
his name is "Ut" (risen up),
for he has risen up above all evils.
Verily, he who knows this rises up above all evils. ChUp 1.6.7.
The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are its two songs;
therefore it is the *udgītha*,
and for that very reason, the *udgātṛ* priest [is so called].
For he is the singer of this [Sāman].
He is the ruler of those worlds which are beyond that [sun] and of the desires of the gods.
Thus far with respect to the divine. (ChU 1.6.8)
Now with reference to the self:
speech indeed is the Ṛg,
and breath is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc. That [Ṛc] is indeed Speech.
The out-breath is *ama*;
that is the *sāman*.
The eye is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the self is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc; the eye is indeed the Sāman,
and the self is the Āma.
That is the Sāman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.2)
The ear is indeed the Ṛg,
and the mind is the Sāman;
thus this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛg.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The ear indeed is the Sāman; the mind is the Amah.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.7.3.
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *ṛc*;
and that which is the dark, intensely black [light] is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the Sāman;
and that which is the dark, the deep black, is the Āma.
That is Sāman. ChUp 1.7.4.
Now, that person who is seen within the eye— he is indeed the Ṛg,
he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha.
That is the Yajus;
that is the Brahman. Of this very [Brahman], its form is the same as the form of that [sun].
Whatever are his joints, those are its joints;
whatever is its name, that is its name.
He is the one who rules over those worlds that are on this side of him, and over the desires of human beings.
Therefore, when these people sing to the lute, they sing to him; hence they are winners of wealth.
Now, he who, knowing it thus, sings this Sāman, sings both.
By means of that [sun] alone, he obtains those worlds which are beyond it, as well as the desires of the gods.
Moreover, by this very [knowledge], he attains those worlds that are on this side of it, as well as the desires of human beings.
Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows this should say: [ChU 1.7.8]
"What desire shall I obtain for you by singing? "For he alone is capable of obtaining desires through his song who, knowing this, sings the Sāman—yes, who sings the Sāman."
There were three who were skilled in the Udgītha: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali.
They said, "We are indeed skilled in the Udgītha; come, let us have a discussion on the Udgītha."
"So be it," they replied and sat down together.
Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said,
"Let the two venerable ones speak first."
"I shall listen to the words of these two wandering mendicants as they speak. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.2)
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "Come, let me question you.
"Ask," he replied.
"What is the goal of the Sāman? "Its goal is tone (svara)," he said. "What is the goal of tone?"
"Life-breath," he said.
"What is the goal of food?
"Food," he said.
"What is the goal of food?
"Water," he said.
"What is the goal of the waters?
"That world," he said.
"What is the goal of that world?"
"It would not lead one to the heavenly world," he said.
"We establish the Sāman upon the heavenly world,
for the Sāman has the heavenly world as its praise."
Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "O Dālbhya, your Sāman is indeed without a foundation.
If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would surely fall off. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.6)
"Ah, let me learn this from the Blessed One.
"Learn it," he said.
"What is the goal of that world? he asked.
"This world," he said. "What is the goal of this world? "One should not lead it beyond its foundation," he said.
"We establish the world as the foundation through the Sāman; for the Sāman is indeed the praise of the foundation. ChUp 1.8.7.
Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him:
"O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite.
If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would fall off."
"Come, let me learn this from the Blessed One.
"Learn it," he said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.8)
"What is the goal of this world?
"Space," he replied.
"Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone."
They pass away into space;
for space is indeed greater than these,
and space is their ultimate resort.
This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high;

this is infinite. For him who, knowing it thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as the higher than the high, there becomes a world higher than the high, and he conquers worlds higher than the high. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2)
Atidhanvan Śaunaka, having taught this very Udgītha to Udara Śāṇḍilya, said:
"As long as they shall know this Udgītha among their offspring, so long will there be for them a superior life in this world."
"Likewise, there will be a world for him in yonder world.

He who, knowing this, meditates upon it—verily, his life in yonder world becomes more excellent, and likewise there is a world for him in yonder world, a world for him in yonder world. Thus ends the section. (ChU 1.9.4)
When the Kuru country was devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived as a beggar in the village of a wealthy man, together with his wife Āṭikī.
He begged from him as he was eating some boiled hemp-seeds.
He said to him,
"There are no others than these which have been set before me."
"Give these to me," he said.
He gave them to him.
"Now, here is a drink for you," [the other said].
"I would indeed have drunk what is left over," he said. (ChU 1.10.3)
"Are these not also leavings?
"I would not have lived without eating them," he said. "Water is my desire. 1.10.4.
Having eaten, he brought the leftovers to his wife;
even before they had been consumed, she became well-supplied with food.
Having received them, she set them aside.
As he was rising in the morning, he said:
"If only we could obtain some food! We might obtain a measure of wealth;
this king is going to perform a sacrifice."
"Let him choose me for all the priestly offices."
His wife said to him,
"Come now, eat these very beans. Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice which was being performed.
There he sat down near the Udgātṛ priests as they were about to chant the Stotra.
He then said to the Prastotṛ: ||| ChUp 1.10.8 |||
"O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will shatter apart. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.9)
In the same way, he said to the Udgātṛ:
"O Udgātṛ, if you perform the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will shatter apart."
In the same way, he said to the Pratihartṛ:
"O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will shatter apart.
Terrified, they remained silent.
Then the sacrificer said to him,
"I desire to know you, O Blessed One.
He replied, "I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa."
He said:
"I have indeed sought you, O Blessed One, for all these priestly offices;
and it was because of my lack of means that I chose others instead of you."
"But let the Blessed One himself perform all the priestly offices for me.
"So be it," [he replied].
"In that case, let these very priests, being fully authorized, perform the praise."
"As long as you give wealth to these [priests], so much should you give to me.
"So be it," the sacrificer replied.
Then the Prastotṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you told me, 'O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will fall off.
Which is that deity? ChU 1.11.4.
"It is *prāṇa*," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings enter into *prāṇa* alone,
and from *prāṇa* they emerge."
This very deity is connected with the Prastāva.
If you had chanted the Prastāva without knowing it, your head would have fallen off, as I have told you.
Then the Udgātṛ approached him and said, "Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is associated with the Udgītha, your head will fall off.
Which is that deity? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.6)
"It is Āditya," he said.
"Indeed, all these beings sing to Āditya as he is high above.
This deity is connected with the Udgītha."
"If you had sung that [hymn] without knowing it while facing northward, your head would have fallen off, even though you were told so by me."
Then the Pratihartṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you perform the Pratihāra without knowing the deity that is connected with the Pratihāra, your head will fall off.
Which is that deity? 1.11.8.
"Food," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings live by taking up food alone.
This deity is dependent upon the Pratihāra."
"If you had brought it back without knowing this, your head would have fallen off—just as I have told you, just as I have told you. (ChU 1.11.9)
Now, therefore, follows the Udgītha of the dogs.
Once, Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—went out to recite his private Vedic study.
For him, a white dog appeared.
Other dogs approached it and said,
"May the venerable one sing for us food."
"Or rather, it is hunger," he said. (ChU 1.12.2)
He said to them, "Come to me right here tomorrow morning.
Then Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, as he was also called—waited there.
Just as those who are about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna laud proceed by holding hands and moving together, even so did they move;
and having sat down together, they uttered the sound "hiṅ."
Oṃ 3 pibā 3 ma.
Oṃ 3. The god Varuṇa, Prajāpati, Savitṛ—may they bring food here.
This world indeed is the syllable *hāuk*.
The syllable *hā* is Vāyu;
the syllable *atha* is the Moon;
the syllable *iha* is the Self.
Agni is the syllable *ī*. ChUp 1.13.1.
Āditya is the syllable ū;
Nihava is the syllable e;
the Viśve Devāḥ are the syllable auho-ī.
Prajāpati is the *hiṅkāra*;
breath is the *svara*;
food is the *yā*.
Speech is Virāj.
The thirteenth is the undefined stobha, the moving syllable *huṃ*.
Speech milks for him that which is the milk of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food— he who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Sāmans, who knows the secret doctrine.
Indeed, the meditation on the entire Sāman is excellent.
For what is excellent, they call "Sāman"; and what is not excellent, they call "Asāman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)
Regarding this, they also say: "He has approached him with the *sāman*"; by this they mean "He has approached him in a good way.
Or they say: "He has approached him without the *sāman*"; by this they mean exactly that.
Then they also say: "It is *sāman* for us, alas! when something is good; they mean to say, "It is indeed good.
"It is not *sāman* for us, alas! when something is not good; they mean to say, "It is indeed not good."
He who, knowing this thus, reveres it as "the good Sāman," will soon find that good qualities come to him and incline toward him.
One should venerate the Sāman in five forms within the worlds:
the earth is the *hiṅkāra*,
and fire is the *prastāva*.
The intermediate space is the *udgītha*;
the sun is the *pratihāra*;
the sky is the *nidhana*.
Thus with respect to the higher worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1)
Now, regarding the unobstructed [worlds]:
the sky is the *hiṅkāra*;
the sun is the *prastāva*.
The intermediate space is the Udgītha;
fire is the Pratihāra;
the earth is the Nidhana.
The worlds, both ascending and descending, become favorable to him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain:
the preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*;
the cloud that arises is the *prastāva*.
When it rains, that is the Udgītha;
when it flashes and thunders, that is the Pratihāra.
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain, takes hold of that finale and indeed causes it to rain. ChUp 2.3.2.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters:
that which clouds gather is the *hiṅkāra*;
that which rains is the *prastāva*.
Those rivers that flow eastward are the *udgītha*; those that flow westward are the *pratihāra*;
the ocean is the *nidhana*.
He does not perish in water; he becomes possessed of water—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons:
spring is the *hiṅkāra*,
summer is the *prastāva*.
The rainy season is the Udgītha;
the autumn is the Pratihāra;
the winter is the Nidhana.
The seasons serve him; he becomes possessed of the seasons, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals:
the goat is the *hiṅkāra*,
and the sheep is the *prastāva*.
Cows are the Udgītha;
the horse is the Pratihāra;
man is the Nidhana.
