When lightning is satisfied, whatever lightning and rain preside over is satisfied;
following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Then, that which he should offer as the fifth, let him offer with: "Svāhā to the out-breath (udāna)! The out-breath becomes satisfied. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.23.1)
When the udāna is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; when the skin is satisfied, the wind is satisfied;
when the wind is satisfied, space is satisfied;
when space is satisfied, whatever the wind and space preside over is satisfied.
Following his satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
If one who does not know this offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, it would be as if he were to remove the live coals and offer the oblation in ashes. 5.24.1.
Now, for one who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.
Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so are all the evils of one who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra oblation consumed.

Therefore, indeed, if one who knows this should give even the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla, it would be as if he had offered it into his own self, into Vaiśvānara. Regarding this, there is this verse: ChUp 5.24.4.
Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother,
so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra sacrifice.
There was once Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi.
His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student.
For, my dear, no one from our family has ever been like a mere kinsman of Brahmins without having studied the Vedas."

Having approached [as a student] at twelve years of age, he returned at twenty-four years of age, having studied all the Vedas; being high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant, he came home.
His father said to him: *Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2*
"Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are now so high-minded, considering yourself well-versed in the Vedas, and so arrogant—

have you perhaps asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? How, indeed, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about?"

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—so it is. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4)

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nugget of gold, everything made of gold would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'gold' alone is the reality. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.5)
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron might be known—
the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'iron' alone is the truth—
so, my dear, is that instruction. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6)
"Surely those venerable ones did not know this;
for if they had known it, why would they not have told it to me?
Let the venerable one himself tell it to me."
"So be it," he said, "O Soma."
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
Regarding this, some say: 'In the beginning, this was Non-being alone, one only, without a second;
from that Non-being, Being was born. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)
"But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? he said.
"How could being be born from non-being? Verily, my dear, in the beginning this was Being alone—one only, without a second."
It thought: "May I become many; may I procreate.
It emitted heat.
That heat (tejas) thought:
"May I become many; may I procreate.
It emitted the waters (ap).
Therefore, wherever a person grieves or perspires, from that very heat water is produced.
Indeed, for these beings there are only three origins: the egg-born, the living-born, and the soil-born.
That deity thought:
"Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate names and forms. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2)
"Let me make each of these three deities threefold.
This very deity, having entered into these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), differentiated names and forms.
Of these, he made each one threefold.
"Now, my dear, learn from me how each of these three deities becomes threefold. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.4)
That which is the red form of Agni is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The nature of fire has departed from fire; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. "The three forms"—that alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The nature of the sun has departed from the sun;
it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of the moon is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The moonhood of the moon has departed.
Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of lightning is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The lightning-nature of lightning has vanished;
it is a modification, a mere handle of speech, a mere name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
Knowing this, indeed, those of old—the great householders and the great Vedic scholars—used to say:
"Nowadays, no one will be able to cite anything to us that we have not heard, have not thought, or have not understood.
For they had gained such knowledge from these [teachers].

"That which appeared as if red—that they recognized as the form of fire; that which appeared as if white—that they recognized as the form of water; and that which appeared as if black—that they recognized as the form of food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.6)
Or, as for that which seemed unintelligible, they understood it to be the combination of these very deities.
"Now, my dear, learn from me how each of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7)
Food that has been eaten is divided into three parts:
its coarsest constituent becomes feces;
its middle constituent becomes flesh.
That which is the subtlest is the mind.
The water that is drunk becomes divided into three parts:
its coarsest constituent becomes urine;
its middle constituent becomes blood.
That which is the subtlest is the vital breath (prāṇa).
The consumed fire is divided into three parts:
its grossest constituent becomes bone;
that which is middling becomes marrow.
That which is the subtlest is speech.
"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
the vital breath consists of water;
and speech consists of fire."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].
"So be it, Somya," he replied.
"O Somya, when curd is being churned, that subtlest part which rises upward becomes ghee. (ChU 6.6.1)
In the very same way, my dear, when food is eaten, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
it becomes the mind.
"Of the waters, my dear, when they are drunk, that which is their subtlest essence rises upward;
it becomes breath."
Of the fire, my dear, being consumed, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
that becomes speech.
"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
breath consists of water;
and speech consists of fire."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].
"So be it, Soma," he replied.
"O gentle one, a person consists of sixteen parts.
Do not eat for fifteen days;
you may drink water as you wish."
"The vital breath consists of water; it will not cease for one who drinks. Thus [he said]. (ChU 6.7.1)
He did not eat for fifteen days.
Then he approached him and said, "Sir, what shall I recite?
[The father replied: "The Ṛg-verses, my dear, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants."
He said, "Indeed, sir, they do not occur to me."

He said to him: "Just as, my dear, if from a large kindled fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left remaining, it would not burn much more than that; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts, only one part remains."
"Therefore, you do not experience the Vedas now. Eat; then you will understand them from me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.7.3)
He was indeed delighted.
Then he approached him;
whatever he asked him, he understood it all.

He said to him: "Just as, my dear, if from a large blazing fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left, and one were to kindle it by adding grass to it, it would burn much more than before—
even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts, only one part remained."
When it was properly nourished with food, it blazed up;
by means of that, you now experience the Vedas.
For, my dear, the mind consists of food.
"Breath consists of water;
speech consists of fire.
He understood this from him—yes, he understood it. Thus ends the sixth section of the sixth chapter.
Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: "My dear, learn from me the state of deep sleep.
When a person here is said to be 'sleeping,' then, my dear, he has become united with Being;
he has gone back into his own self."
Therefore, they say of him,
"He sleeps," for he has gone into his own (svam).
"Just as a bird tied by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down at its very bond;
even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down in the vital breath (prāṇa).
For the mind, my dear, is fastened to the vital breath. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2)
"Understand from me, my dear, hunger and thirst.
When a person is said to be 'hungry,' it is the waters that lead away what has been eaten.
Just as one says 'cow-leader,' 'horse-leader,' or 'man-leader,' so they call water 'aśanāya' (the leader of food)."
"In this regard, my dear, understand that this sprout has emerged;
it cannot be without a root. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3)
"Where could its root be, if not in food? In this very way, my dear, seek water as the root by means of food as the sprout; seek fire as the root by means of water as the sprout."
"My dear, seek the root of Being by means of the sprout that is fire.
My dear, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support."
Now, when a person is said to be thirsty, it is the fire itself that leads away what has been drunk.
Just as one says "cow-leader," "horse-leader," or "man-leader," so does one designate that fire as "water.
In this regard, my dear, understand that this very thing which has sprouted forth is the shoot.
"This shall not be without foundation. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.5)
Where could its root be, other than in water? My dear, seek the root of heat through the sprout that is water;
my dear, seek the root of Being through the sprout that is heat.
"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being (sat) as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support.
Now, O gentle one, it has already been explained how each of these three divinities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold, threefold.

When this person departs, O gentle one, speech merges into the mind; the mind merges into the vital breath (prāṇa); the vital breath merges into heat (tejas); and heat merges into the highest divinity."
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further," he said.
"So be it, my dear," he replied.
"Just as, my dear, honey-making bees prepare honey, bringing together the juices of trees of various kinds and reducing them to a single essence. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.1)

Just as those juices there do not obtain distinction, thinking, "I am the juice of this tree; I am the juice of that tree," even so, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know, "We are merging into Being."
Whatever they become here—whether a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gadfly, or a mosquito—that they become.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further," he said.
"So be it, my son," he replied.
"O dear one, these rivers flow eastward from the front and westward from behind;
they go from the ocean back into the very ocean,
and they become the ocean itself."
Just as there, they do not know, "I am this," or "I am that."
In just this way, my dear, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know that they are coming from Being.
Whatever they are here—whether a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—that they become, that they return to.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further," [he said].
"So be it, my dear," he replied.

"My dear, if one were to strike this great tree at its root, it would continue to exude sap while living; if one were to strike it in the middle, it would continue to exude sap while living; if one were to strike it at the top, it would continue to exude sap while living.
Pervaded by this living self, it stands drinking deeply and rejoicing."
When the living soul leaves one branch of this tree, that branch withers; when it leaves a second, that branch withers;
when it leaves a third, that branch withers.
Everyone abandons everything; everyone withers away.
"In this very way, my dear, understand it," he said.
"Truly, it is only when abandoned by the living self (jīva) that this [body] dies; the living self does not die.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self."
"That is the Truth;
that is the Self;
That thou art, Śvetaketu."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].
"So be it, Soma," he replied.
"Bring me a fruit of the banyan tree. "Here it is, Blessed One. "Break it open."
"It is broken, Blessed One.
"What do you see there?
"These grains appear like atoms, Blessed One."
"Break one of these limbs," [he said]. "It is broken, Blessed One.
"What do you see there? he asked.
"Nothing at all, Blessed One," he replied. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.12.1)
He said to him: "My dear Somya, that subtle essence which you do not perceive—it is from this very subtle essence, my dear, that such a great banyan tree stands.
Have faith, my dear!"
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further," he said.
"So be it, my dear," he replied.
"Place this salt in water, and then come to me in the morning.
He did accordingly.
[The teacher] said to him:
"Place salt in water at night, my dear, and bring it to me in the morning.
Having done so, he touched it but did not find it. ChU 6.13.1.
"Just as it has melted away.
[The teacher says: "Rinse your mouth from the edge of your limb.
[The student asks: "How?"
"Salt," he said.
"Rinse your mouth from the middle," he said.
"How? he asked.
"Salt.
"One should sip water from the edge.
"How so?"
"Salt! he said.
"Throw this away, and then come back to me.
He did exactly so.
And that [wind] continues to revolve eternally.
He said to him: "In this very place, my dear, you surely do not perceive that; indeed, it is right here."
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.

"Just as, my dear, if one were to bring a man from the Gandhāras with his eyes bound and then leave him in a deserted place—he would, there, with his eyes still bound, cry out, 'I have been brought here with my eyes bound; I have been left here with my eyes bound,' whether he was facing east, north, south, or west. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.1)
Just as one might untie his blindfold and tell him, "The Gandhārans are in this direction;
go in that direction," he, being wise and intelligent, by asking from village to village, would eventually arrive at the Gandhārans;
even so does a person who has a teacher know here.
"For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he will attain [perfection]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2)
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Venerable sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.
"O gentle one, when a person is afflicted by illness, his kinsmen sit around him and say, 'Do you know me? Do you know me?
As long as his speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity, so long does he know. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.15.1)
Then, when his speech is merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the highest deity, then he no longer knows.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further," [he said].
"So be it, my dear," he replied.
"O Somya, they bring a man, seized by the hand, saying:
'He has stolen; he has committed theft; heat the axe for him!
If he is the doer of that deed, then he makes himself false."
He who intends falsely, having concealed himself with falsehood, takes up the heated axe;
he is burned and then slain. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.1)
Then, if he is not the doer of that [crime],
he thereby makes himself true.
Being committed to truth, having concealed himself by means of truth, he takes up the heated axe.
He is not burned;
then he is released.
Just as he would not be burned there,
so too this whole world has that as its self;
that is the truth.
"That is the Self;
that art thou, Śvetaketu. Then he understood it from him—yes, he understood it. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.3)
"Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, saying, 'Teach me, O Venerable One.
He said to him, 'Approach me with what you already know;
then I shall tell you what lies beyond that.'"
He said: "ChUp 7.1.1"

"Venerable Sir, I have studied the Rigveda; the Yajurveda; the Samaveda; the Atharvana as the fourth; the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas; the science of ancestral rites; the science of numbers; the science of portents; the science of treasures; the science of argumentation; the science of monism; the science of the gods;

the science of sacred formulation (*brahmavidyā*); the science of elemental beings; the science of government; the science of the stars; and the science of serpents and celestial beings—this much, Venerable Sir, [I have studied]."
I meditate upon it. ChUp 7.1.2.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I am indeed a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self.
For I have heard from those like your reverence that "the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
Thus, O Blessed One, I am in sorrow.
"May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow.
He said to him: "Whatever you have studied here, that is indeed only name."
Namely: the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth, the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas,

the Veda of the Vedas, the Pitrya, the Rashis, the Daiva, the Nidhi, the Vakovakya, the Ekayana, the Devavidya, the Brahmavidya, the Bhutavidya, the Kshatravidya, the Nakshatravidya, and the Sarpadevajanavidya.
"It is merely Name. Meditate upon Name. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.4)
He who meditates on "Name" as Brahman—
so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom, provided he meditates on "Name" as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than Name?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than name. May the Blessed One tell me that."

Speech is indeed greater than name. Speech, indeed, makes known the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of the ancestors, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, etymology, phonology, the science of the gods, and the science of ritual.

The knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of beings, the knowledge of the ruling power, the knowledge of the stars, the knowledge of serpents and divine beings; heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire; gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey, down to insects, moths, and ants; and both righteousness and unrighteousness.
"Speech indeed makes known both truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, that which is pleasing to the heart and that which is not.

For if speech did not exist, neither dharma nor adharma would be made known; neither truth nor falsehood, neither the good nor the bad, neither that which is pleasing to the heart nor that which is not.
Speech alone makes all this known. Venerate speech! (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.1)
He who venerates speech as Brahman—
so far as speech extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who venerates speech as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than speech?"
"Verily, there is something greater than speech. May the Blessed One tell that to me."
The mind, indeed, is greater than speech.
Just as one's fist encompasses two *vāmalaka* fruits, or two *kola* fruits, or two *akṣa* fruits, even so the mind encompasses both speech and name.
When one intends with the mind, "I would study the sacred hymns," then one studies them.
Thinking, "I shall perform actions," he then performs them;
thinking, "I shall desire sons and cattle," he then desires them; thinking, "I shall desire this world and that world," he then desires them.
For the mind is the self;
for the mind is the world;
for the mind is Brahman.
"Meditate upon the mind," he said.
He who venerates the mind as Brahman—
so far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who venerates the mind as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than the mind?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than the mind. May the Blessed One tell me that. 7.3.2.
Volition is indeed greater than the mind.
For when one wills, then one thinks;
then one utters speech.
And they lead her to the name;
for the mantras become one in the name, and the ritual acts are contained within the mantras. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.4.1)
Indeed, these have intention as their sole path, they consist of intention, and they are established in intention.
Heaven and earth were intended;
wind and space were intended.
Heat and radiance were formed together;
through their formation, rain was formed;
through the formation of rain, food was formed.
Through the intentionality of food, the vital breaths become intentional; through the intentionality of the vital breaths, the mantras become intentional;
through the intentionality of the mantras, ritual actions become intentional.
Through the volitional determination of actions, the world is determined; through the volitional determination of the world, everything is determined.
This is that very volitional determination.
"Meditate upon intention."—ChU 7.4.2.
He who meditates on volition as Brahman attains worlds that are fashioned, stable, firmly established, unshakable, and free from distress; he himself becomes stable and unshakable.
As far as the reach of volition extends, so far he has freedom of movement, provided that he meditates on volition as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than volition?
"There is indeed something greater than volition.
"May the Venerable Sir explain that to me."
The mind is indeed greater than volition.
For when one perceives, then one wills;
then one reflects.
Then he utters speech;
he leads that [speech] into the name.
In the name, the mantras become one.
Ritual actions are contained within the mantras.
These, indeed, have thought as their single path, thought as their self, and are established in thought.

Therefore, even if one who possesses many kinds of knowledge becomes devoid of thought, they say of him: "This man does not exist. For they think: "If he were truly learned, he would not be thus devoid of thought."
Now, if one possesses a mind of little insight, people listen to him only from that [limited perspective];
for the mind alone is their single path,
and the mind is their self.
"The mind is the foundation;
meditate upon the mind. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.5.2)

He who meditates on Brahman as the mind (citta) indeed attains worlds that are steadfast, being himself steadfast; established, being himself established; unshakable, being himself unshakable. As far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on Brahman as the mind.
"Is there, Blessed One, anything greater than the mind?
"There is indeed something greater than the mind. "May the Blessed One tell me that. 7.5.3.
Meditation is indeed greater than thought.
The earth, as it were, meditates; the intermediate space, as it were, meditates.
The sky, as it were, meditates; the waters, as it were, meditate; the mountains, as it were, meditate.
Gods and humans seem as if they were meditating;
therefore, those among humans here who attain greatness become, as it were, participants in the attainment of meditation.
But those who are few, quarrelsome, slanderous, and backbiters—[they are otherwise].
Then those who are capable become like the constituent parts of the attainment of meditation;
[the teacher says to them: "Meditate upon meditation. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.6.1)

He who worships meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as Brahman— so far as the reach of meditative concentration extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who worships meditative concentration as Brahman. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than meditative concentration?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than meditation.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Consciousness, indeed, is greater than meditation.

By means of consciousness, one discerns the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaṇa* as the fourth, the *Itihāsa-purāṇa* as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, the science of the gods, the science of spirits, the science of snakes, and the science of celestial bodies.

The knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of beings, the knowledge of the Kṣatra, the knowledge of the stars, the knowledge of serpents and divine beings; heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire; gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey, down to worms, moths, and ants.

"By means of consciousness alone one discerns both dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, that which is pleasing to the heart and that which is not, food and its flavor, and this world and the next; therefore, venerate consciousness. (ChU 7.7.1)
He who meditates on consciousness as Brahman attains worlds that are indeed possessed of consciousness and knowledge.
As far as the reach of consciousness extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on consciousness as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than consciousness?
"There is indeed something greater than consciousness.
"May the Venerable Sir explain that to me."
Power, indeed, is greater than consciousness.
For even a single powerful man can shake a hundred men possessed of consciousness.
When he possesses power, then he becomes one who can rise up.
Rising up, one becomes an attendant; attending, one becomes a follower;
following closely, one becomes a beholder, a hearer, a thinker, an awakener, an agent, and a knower.

By strength indeed the earth stands; by strength the atmosphere, by strength the sky; by strength the mountains, by strength gods and humans, by strength beasts and birds, grasses, trees, and wild animals—even down to worms, moths, and ants. By strength the world stands.
"Venerate strength."—Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.8.1.
He who worships strength—
so far as strength extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who worships strength as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than strength?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than strength.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Food, indeed, is greater than strength;
therefore, even if one were not to eat for ten nights,
one might nevertheless continue to live.
Or else, when there is no food, one becomes a non-seer, a non-hearer, a non-thinker, a non-understander, a non-doer, and a non-perceiver.
But when there is food, one becomes a seer, one becomes a hearer, one becomes a thinker, one becomes an understander, one becomes a doer, and one becomes a perceiver.
"Meditate upon food," he said.
He who meditates on food as Brahman attains worlds rich in food and drink.
As far as the reach of food extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on food as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything more than food?
"There is indeed something more than food. "May the Venerable Sir tell that to me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.9.2)
Water, indeed, is greater than food.
Therefore, when there is no good rain, living beings suffer, thinking, "Food will become scarce.
But when there is good rain, living beings rejoice, thinking, "Food will become abundant."

"Water alone is this in its solidified form: that which is this earth, that which is the intermediate space, that which is the sky, that which are the mountains, that which are gods and humans, that which are beasts and birds, the grasses, the trees, the wild animals, down to the worms, moths, and ants—water alone is these in their solidified form.
Meditate upon water. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.10.1)
He who meditates on water as Brahman obtains all desires and becomes satisfied. As far as the reach of water extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on water as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than water?
"There is indeed something greater than water.
"May the venerable sir tell me that."
Fire, indeed, is greater than water.
Having seized the wind, it heats the space; then people say, "It is glowing, it is scorching; it will rain.
Fire, having first displayed itself, then creates water.
Therefore, with these lightning flashes moving upward and across, the peals of thunder proceed; hence they say, "It lightens, it thunders, it will rain.
Having first displayed its brilliance, it then emits water.
Meditate upon brilliance.
He who meditates upon fire as Brahman becomes indeed radiant;
he attains radiant worlds that are luminous and free from darkness.
As far as fire extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon fire as Brahman.
"Venerable sir, is there anything greater than heat?
"There is indeed something greater than heat.
"May the venerable sir explain that to me."
Space, indeed, is greater than fire.
In space, indeed, are both the sun and the moon, lightning, the stars, and fire.
By means of space, one calls out.
He hears with space;
he responds with space;
he delights in space.
It does not delight in space;
it is born in space;
it is born from space.
"Meditate upon space. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.12.1)
He who meditates on space as Brahman attains worlds that possess space, that are luminous, unconfined, and vast;
as far as space extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on space as Brahman.
"Is there, Blessed One, anything greater than space?
"There is indeed something greater than space. "May the Blessed One tell that to me."
Memory, indeed, is greater than space.
Therefore, even if many were to sit together, if they were not mindful, they would not hear anything, they would not think, and they would not understand.
But when they become mindful, then they hear, then they think, and then they understand.
"By memory one indeed knows one's sons; by memory one knows one's cattle.
Meditate upon memory. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.13.1)
He who meditates on memory as Brahman—
so far as memory extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on memory as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than memory?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than memory.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Hope, indeed, is greater than memory.
For one who is kindled by hope studies the sacred hymns, performs ritual acts, desires sons and cattle, and desires both this world and the world beyond.
Meditate upon hope.
He who meditates on hope as Brahman—
his every desire is fulfilled through hope,
and his prayers never go in vain.
As far as hope extends, so far he has freedom of movement who meditates upon hope as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than hope? "There is something greater than hope."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. (ChU 7.14.2)
Breath indeed is greater than hope.
Just as spokes are fixed in the hub, so everything is fixed in this breath.
Breath moves by means of breath.
The vital breath gives life;
it gives unto life;
the vital breath is indeed the father.
The vital breath is the mother;
the vital breath is the brother;
the vital breath is the sister.
The vital breath is the teacher;
the vital breath is the Brahmin.

If he should speak harshly to his father, or mother, or brother, or sister, or teacher, or a Brahmin, they say to him: "Fie upon you! You are indeed a patricide; you are indeed a matricide; you are indeed a fratricide; you are indeed a sororicide; you are indeed a slayer of your teacher; you are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.2)

Now, even if one were to burn these [bodies], whose vital breaths have departed, all at once with a poker, they would not say of him: "You are a slayer of your father," nor "a slayer of your mother," nor "a slayer of your brother," nor "a slayer of your sister," nor "a slayer of your teacher," nor "a slayer of a Brahmin. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.3)
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed becomes all these things.
He who sees thus, thinks thus, and knows thus, becomes a transcendent speaker (*ativādī*).
If they should say to him, "Are you a transcendent speaker? [he should reply: "I am a transcendent speaker."
He should say, "I am an over-speaker," and he should not deny it.
"But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of truth.
I, O Venerable Sir, am one who speaks transcendentally by means of truth.
"But truth itself, indeed, must be sought to be known."
"Venerable sir, I desire to know the truth," [he said].
When one truly understands, then one speaks the truth;
one who does not understand does not speak the truth;
only one who understands speaks the truth.
"But consciousness itself is what one must desire to understand.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand consciousness."
When one indeed thinks, then one understands;
one does not understand without having thought;
it is only by having thought that one understands.
"But intelligence itself is what one should desire to understand. "Venerable sir, I desire to understand intelligence. 7.18.1.
When one indeed has faith, then one reflects;
one who lacks faith does not reflect;
only one who has faith reflects.
"But faith itself is what one must desire to understand.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand faith. 7.19.1.
When one indeed perseveres, then one has faith;
one who does not persevere does not have faith. Only by persevering does one have faith.
"But the culmination itself is what must be sought to be known.
"Venerable sir, I wish to know the culmination."
When one acts, then one completes;
one does not complete without having acted;
only by having acted does one complete.
"But one must desire to understand action itself.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand action."
When one indeed attains happiness, then one acts; having not attained happiness, one does not act.
Only after attaining happiness does one act.
"But bliss indeed is what one should desire to understand.
"I desire to understand bliss, O Venerable Sir."
That which is indeed the plenum is happiness;
there is no happiness in the finite;
the plenum alone is happiness.
"But the Plenum itself is what one should desire to understand.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand the Plenum."
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman).
But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpa).
Verily, that which is the Infinite is the Immortal.
"Now, that which is small is mortal.
In what, O Venerable Sir, is it established?
"In its own greatness, or perhaps not even in greatness."
"Cows and horses here they call 'greatness,' as do elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, and dwellings.
"I do not say so," he said. "I do say so," he replied.
For one is established in the other. // ChUp 7.24.2 //
He alone is below, He is above, He is behind, He is in front, He is to the south, He is to the north;
He alone is all this. Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the "I-maker" (ahaṃkāra).
"I alone am below, I am above; I am behind, I am in front; I am to the south, I am to the north—I indeed am all this. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1)
Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the Self alone:
"The Self alone is below; the Self is above; the Self is behind; the Self is in front; the Self is to the south; the Self is to the north; the Self indeed is all this.
He who sees thus, who thinks thus, and who understands thus, finds delight in the Self, sports with the Self, has union with the Self, and rejoices in the Self; he becomes a self-ruler.
He has freedom of movement in all worlds.
But those who know otherwise than this are subject to other rulers; their worlds are perishable, and they have no freedom of movement in any world. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2)
For him who sees thus, who reflects thus, and who understands thus—verily, from the Self comes breath;
from the Self comes hope; from the Self comes memory; from the Self comes space; from the Self comes fire; from the Self come the waters; from the Self come manifestation and disappearance;
from the Self comes food; from the Self comes strength; from the Self comes perception; from the Self comes meditation; from the Self comes thought; from the Self comes volition.
"The mind is from the Self; speech is from the Self; name is from the Self; sacred hymns are from the Self; ritual acts are from the Self; indeed, all this is from the Self alone.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1)
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering.
The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way."
Thus,
he becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, five-fold, seven-fold, nine-fold, and again he is recorded as eleven-fold.
One hundred and ten, and twenty thousand;
through purity of food comes purity of being;
through purity of being, mindfulness becomes firm.
Upon attaining mindfulness, there is the complete release from all knots of the heart.
To him whose impurities have been rubbed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness;
they call him Skanda.
Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; within it is a small space.
That which is inside that [space] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. (ChU 8.1.1)

If they should say to him: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space (ākāśa). What is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand? he should reply: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.2.
As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart.
Both heaven and earth are contained within it;
both fire and wind, both sun and moon, as well as lightning and the stars.
"Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have—all that is contained within this. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3)

If they should say to him: "If everything is contained within this city of Brahman—namely, all beings and all desires—and if it is overtaken by old age or perishes, what remains of it? [he should reply:
He should say:
"This does not age with his aging; it is not slain by his being slain.
This is the true city of Brahman; within it, all desires are contained."
This Self is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst; its desires are true, its resolves are true.
Just as subjects here follow according to instruction, so they enter upon whatever end they desire—whatever region or whatever portion of land—and upon that very thing they subsist.

Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so there the world won by merit perishes. Therefore, those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is no freedom of movement in any of the worlds. But those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all the worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6)
If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers,
his fathers arise by his mere volition;
endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of mothers,
by his mere volition mothers arise for him;
endowed with that world of mothers, he is magnified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers,
his brothers arise for him by mere resolve;
endowed with that world of brothers, he prospers.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of sisters, by his mere volition sisters arise for him;
endowed with that world of sisters, he thrives in greatness.
Now, if he desires the world of friends,
his friends arise for him by his mere resolve; endowed with that world of friends, he rejoices.
Now, if he desires the world of perfumes and garlands,
by his mere volition, perfumes and garlands arise for him;
endowed with that world of perfumes and garlands, he is magnified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of food and drink, by his mere volition food and drink arise for him;
endowed with that world of food and drink, he is magnified.
Now, if he has a desire for the world of song and instrumental music, by his mere volition, song and instrumental music arise for him;
endowed with that world of song and instrumental music, he rejoices.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of women, women arise for him by his mere will;
endowed with that world of women, he rejoices.
Whatever end he desires,
whatever wish he wishes for, that arises for him by his mere volition alone.
Endowed with that, he is glorified.
These true desires have untruth as their covering.
Untruth is the covering for those true [desires] that exist;
for whoever departs from here does not obtain them here for the purpose of seeing.
Now, whatever living beings belong to him here, and those who have departed, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain—all that he finds upon going there.
For here, indeed, these true desires of his are covered by untruth.
It is just as if people ignorant of the location were to pass repeatedly over a hidden treasure of gold and not find it.
In this very way, all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it, for they are held back by untruth.
This very Self is in the heart. This is its etymological explanation: "He is here in the heart" (hṛdi ayam), therefore he is called "the one in the heart" (hṛdayam).
Day after day, one who knows this goes to the heavenly world.
Then he said: "That serene being who, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, appears in his own true form—that is the Self.
This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
And the name of this very Brahman is "Truth."
Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support, for the non-separation of these worlds.
Day and night do not cross this bridge, nor do old age, death, sorrow, or merit.
All evils turn back from it.
For this world of Brahman is indeed free from evil.
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even if he is blind, he becomes sighted; even if he is pierced, he becomes unpierced; even if he is afflicted by disease, he becomes free from affliction.
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even at night one arrives at day alone;
for this world of Brahman is indeed always shining.
Therefore, those who find this world of Brahman through celibacy—for them alone is this world of Brahman;
for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.
Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (yajña) is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya);
for by means of celibacy alone does the knower find that [Brahman].
And that which they call "the performed sacrifice" (iṣṭa) is indeed celibacy.
For it is by means of the practice of celibacy that one, having performed sacrifice, finds the Self.

Now, that which they call the *sattrāyaṇa* sacrifice is simply celibacy (*brahmacarya*); for by means of celibacy alone does one find protection for the existing self. And that which they call "silence" (*mauna*) is simply celibacy.
For it is indeed by means of the holy life (brahmacarya) that one finds and reflects upon the Self.
Now, that which they call "the path of non-destruction" is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
for this Self does not perish, which one finds through celibacy.
And that which they call "the path of the forest" is indeed celibacy.
Now, Ara and Nya are two oceans in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here;
there is the lake Airammadīya,
and there is the Aśvattha tree called Somasavana.
That is the invincible city of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord.
Therefore, those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)—to them alone belongs this world of Brahman;
for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.
Now, these channels of the heart—those of the minute, tawny-colored [substance], and those of the white, the blue, the yellow, and the red—correspond to this sun:
it is tawny, it is white, it is blue, it is yellow, and it is red.
Just as a great highway stretches out and goes to both villages—this one and that one—even so these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one.
They extend from yonder sun and have entered into these channels;
they extend from these channels and have entered into yonder sun.
When, being thus asleep, composed, and serene, one does not perceive any dream,
then he has entered into these channels;
no evil whatsoever touches him.
For at that time, he becomes endowed with splendor.
Then, when he has been reduced to weakness, those sitting around him say, "Do you know me? Do you know me?
as long as he has not yet departed from this body.
Only so much does he know. ChUp 8.6.4.
Now, when he departs from this body,
he ascends upwards by means of these very rays;
he passes away either saying "Om" or simply "Hā."
As quickly as one can turn the mind, so swiftly does it go to the sun.
This, indeed, is the gate to the world, the entrance for the wise, and the obstruction for the ignorant.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; one of them extends up to the crown of the head.
Moving upward through that, one attains immortality; the others lead in all directions for departing, for departing. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6)

"That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," so indeed said Prajāpati.
Both the gods and the asuras became aware of this.
They said, "Come, let us seek that Self, by seeking which one obtains all worlds and all desires.
Of them, Indra went forth among the gods, and Virocana among the asuras.
The two of them, not being in agreement with each other, approached Prajāpati with sacrificial fuel in their hands.
The two of them lived as religious students for thirty-two years.
Prajāpati said to them: "Desiring what have you dwelt here?"

They both said: "That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires—such is the word of the venerable ones they proclaim. Desiring that, we have come here. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3)
Prajāpati said to them both: "This person who is seen in the eye—this is the Self," he said.
"This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Then [Naciketas asked]: "Venerable sir, that which is perceived in the water and that which is perceived in a mirror—which one is this?"
"This very one, indeed, is perceived within all these ends," he said.
"Look at yourselves in a bowl of water; whatever you do not understand of yourselves, tell that to me.
The two of them looked into the bowl of water.
Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see?"
They both said, "O Venerable One, we see this entire self of ours exactly as it is, even down to the hair and the nails. ChU 8.8.1.
Prajāpati said to them both, "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look into a pan of water.
Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, they both looked into the pan of water.
Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see?"
They both said, "Venerable sir, just as we here are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed, even so these two, venerable sir, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed.
He said, "This is the Self;
this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
With their hearts at peace, the two of them departed.
Having observed them both, Prajāpati said:
"If they depart without perceiving the Self and without knowing it, whichever of these two—whether gods or asuras—possess this secret doctrine (upaniṣad), they shall perish.
Then Virocana, with his heart still unappeased, went to the asuras.
To them he proclaimed this secret doctrine (upaniṣad): "The Self alone is to be magnified here; the Self is to be served.
By magnifying the Self alone here and by serving the Self, one attains both worlds—this one and the one beyond. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.8.4)
Therefore, even today, they say of one who does not give here, who lacks faith, and who does not sacrifice, "Alas, he is an Asura!
For this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Asuras:
they adorn the body of the deceased with alms, clothing, and ornaments.
For by this, they think they will conquer that world.
Then Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this fear:

"Just as this [self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-clothed when it is well-clothed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, it becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed."
"Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes;
I see no enjoyment in this," [he said]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.1)
With fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him,
"O Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart along with Virocana, desiring what have you come back?"

He said: "Just as indeed, O Venerable One, this [self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-clad when it is well-clad, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, it becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed."
"Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes;
I see no object of enjoyment here," [he said]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.2)
"It is even so, O Maghavan," he said.
"However, I shall explain this very matter further to you.
Dwell for another thirty-two years."
He lived there for another thirty-two years;
then he said to him:
"That which moves about being honored in a dream—that is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
With his heart calmed, he departed.
But even before reaching the gods, he saw this fear:
"Even if this body is blind, he becomes sighted; if it is lame, he becomes not lame. Indeed, he is not defiled by its defect. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.10.1)
It is not slain by the slaying of this [body], nor is it wounded by the wounding of this;
yet they indeed slay it.
It seems as if it is being covered;
it feels as if it has encountered something unpleasant; it even seems as if it weeps, thinking, "I see nothing here that can be enjoyed. (ChU 8.10.2)
With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him:
"O Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?"
He said:
"Venerable sir, even if this body becomes blind, he remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not lame.
Indeed, he is not affected by its defect."
It is not slain by the slaying of this [body]; it does not waste away by the wasting of this [body]. Yet, they seem to slay it.
It is as if covering [the mind];
it is as if experiencing what is unpleasant;
even so, it is as if weeping.
"I see nothing here to enjoy," [he said].
"Just so, O Maghavan," he replied.
"I shall explain this very same thing to you further."
"Stay for another thirty-two years.
He stayed for another thirty-two years.
Then he said to him:
"Therefore, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
With his heart calmed, he departed.
Not having yet reached the gods, he perceived this danger:
"Indeed, even now one does not know oneself thus: 'This is I';
nor likewise these beings."
"He has gone to utter destruction;
I see nothing here to enjoy," he said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.1)
With fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?
He replied: "Indeed, O Venerable Sir, even now one does not know oneself thus: 'This is I.'"
"In this way, these beings do not exist;
one has simply gone to destruction.
I see nothing here that can be enjoyed. Thus spoke Śāṇḍilya.
"It is even so, O Maghavan," he said.
"I shall explain this very same thing further to you, but not otherwise than this."
"May I dwell for another five years.
He dwelt for another five years;
thus they amounted to one hundred and one.
This is what they say:
"For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Prajāpati.
To him, [Prajāpati] said: ChUp 8.11.3.
O Maghavan, this mortal body is indeed seized by death;
it is the substratum for this immortal, bodiless Self.
For that which possesses a body is indeed seized by pleasure and pain.
"For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant;
but for one who is truly bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1)
The wind is bodiless;
the cloud, lightning, and thunder—these are bodiless.
Just as these, having risen from that space and having reached the highest light, appear in their own forms; so it is with him.
In this very way, this serene being, having arisen from this body and having attained the supreme light, manifests in its own true form. He is the Supreme Person.
There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women, or with carriages, or with kinsmen, no longer remembering this body which has been produced.
Just as a draft animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath (prāṇa) yoked to this body.
Now, where this space has entered into the eye, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing.
Now, he who knows "let me smell this" is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling. Now, he who knows "let me speak this" is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking.
Now, he who knows "may I hear this" is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing.
Now, he who knows "I shall think this" is the Self;
the mind is his divine eye.
Indeed, with that divine eye, the mind, he beholds these desires and rejoices in them which are in the world of Brahman.
The gods indeed worship this very Self;
therefore, all worlds and all desires are attained by them.
He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires.
Thus indeed spoke Prajāpati; Prajāpati spoke.
"From the dark I pass to the speckled; from the speckled I pass to the dark.

Like a horse shaking off its hairs, having shaken off evil, and like the moon freeing itself from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I—being one whose self is perfected—attain the uncreated world of Brahman; yes, I attain it."
Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form;
that which is between them is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Self.
I enter the assembly hall, the abode of Prajāpati. May I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas, the glory of the Kṣatriyas, the glory of the Vaiśyas.
"I have attained glory;
I am indeed the glory of glories.
O white, toothless one, toothless white one, do not approach me with a flow; do not approach me with a flow."
This very [knowledge] Brahmā told to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to Manu; and Manu to his progeny.

Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the prescribed rule, and having returned home with the remainder of the time after performing service for the teacher, one should dwell in a household, reciting the sacred study (*svādhyāya*) in a pure place, establishing virtuous sons, withdrawing all the senses into the self, and practicing non-violence.
Except for those who have reached the sacred shrines (tīrtha), all beings [return].
Indeed, conducting himself thus throughout his life, he attains the world of Brahman;
and he does not return again, he does not return again.
